Nārāyaṇī
(‘the spouse or power of नारायण’)
------------------------------------------
As the very name suggests, she is the शक्ति or female counterpart of नारायण and hence लक्ष्मी herself. Iconographically she is shown just like नारायण or विष्णु.
Nārāyaṇī is a well-known name of दुर्गा too. The Devīmāhātmya contains a long hymn (17.1-35) on नारायणी and is known as the Nārāyaṇīstuti. See DURGĀ for details.
Nārāyaṇī (or Nālāyanī) was also the name of the sage मुद्गल’s wife, her other name being Indrasenā. It was she who was reborn as द्रौपदी in her next birth (vide Mahābhārata, Ādiparva, ch. 212).

Narmadā
(‘giver of joy’)
------------------------------------------
One of the seven sacred rivers of India, remembered daily at the time of ritualistic worship, नर्मदा is said to have been born out of the sweat of Lord शिव when he was once engaged in तपस् or austerities. The goddess of this river was so charmingly beautiful that she gave joy to one and all who saw her. Hence the name नर्मदा.
Though not mentioned in the वेदस्, it has been highly eulogised both in the Mahābhārata and in the पुराणस् like the Matsya, the Kūrma and the Padma.
It has been called ‘Revā’ also, the other names being Somodbhavā and Mekhalakanyakā.
It takes its birth in the mountains of अमरकण्टक (in Madhya Pradesh), flows towards the west and joins the sea near the gulf of Cambay (near Broach, the ancient Bhṛgukaccha). Its total length is 1282 kms. (796 miles). There is one water-falls of 24 metres (80 feet) at Kapiladhārā and of 12 metres (40 ft.) near Jabalpur.
There are many holy spots on the banks of this river like Oṅkārnāth, Karnāli, Śuklatīrtha, Broach and so on. Oṅkārnāth is one of the twelve Jyotirliṇgas and the temple is situated on the island of Māndhātā inside the river. The emperor Māndhātā of the solar race is said to have worshipped this लिङ्ग. The island itself is situated between the rivers नर्मदा and कावेरी (not the कावेरी of South India). It is here that शिव is said to have destroyed the three cities, त्रिपुर.
Bāṇaliṅgas of शिव are available in the river-bed a few miles away from ओङ्कारेश्वर (See BĀṆLIṆGA for details.)
Where the tributary Or merges into Narmadā—the place being called Chandod —Vyāsa is said to have performed auste-rities.
Śrāddhas (obsequial rites) done on the banks of the नर्मदा are said to yield inexhaustible results.
Narmadā-parikrama is another sacred act sometimes undertaken by devout pilgrims. It consists in walking from the confluence at sea up to the source in अमरकण्टक and then return by the other bank to the sea. This generally takes about two years.
In the Śuklatīrtha, there are three ponds of Kavi, Śukla and ओङ्कारेश्वर. A religious festival is held here every year on the pūrṇima or full-मोओन् day of Kārttika.
The Viṣṇupurāṇa (4.3) gives a मन्त्र in praise of नर्मदा which dispels the poisons of serpents.
The water of नर्मदा is considered so pure that even गङ्गा (the goddess of that river) comes once a year as a black cow, bathes in it, becomes white and then returns!
Temples of Kumbheśvara महादेव, शनि (Saturn) and Śūrpaṇeśvara are the other holy places gracing its banks.
See also AMARAKAṆṬAKA.

nārāyaṇabali
(‘offering to [please] नारायण’)
------------------------------------------
The Hindus believe that performing obsequial rites with proper offerings will help the souls or spirits of dead persons in relieving their sufferings and guiding them to the next destination. This becomes all the more necessary if a person has met with an unnatural death by सुइचिदे or accidents.
Nārāyaṇabali is a rite connected with this. It is performed generally on the eleventh day of the bright half of a month, and involves the worship of विष्णु and यम (the god of death). Ten piṇḍas (rice-balls) are placed on the दर्भ (grass—Saccharum cylindricum or Poa cynosuroides), laved with honey. The details of the rite are similar to the एकोद्दिष्ट-śrāddha.
According to some other works like the Antyeṣṭipaddhati of Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa (A. D. 1513-1570?) five kalaśas (pitchers of water) are to be placed on a quantity of rice spread over a leaf on which five images of ब्रह्मा, विष्णु, शिव, यम and that of the dead person are to be drawn. Worship is to be offered through certain mantras of the Ṛgveda (e.g., 10.90). Ten piṇḍas are to be offered and then cast in a river.
See also ŚRĀDDHA.

Narasiṁha
(‘Man-lion [incarnation]’)
------------------------------------------
See AVATĀRA and DAŚĀVATĀRAS.
Independent shrines of नरसिṁह are quite common in South India, whereas he has small shrines or niches in the temples of विष्णु in the North.
Iconographic descriptions of the deity are provided in several āgama treatises like Vihagendrasaṁhitā, Pādma-saṁhitā, Īśvarasaṁhitā, Parāśarasaṁhitā and Sāttvatasaṁhitā.
The forms delineated are too numerous to mention. Some of these are: āsīna (seated); स्थानक (standing); yānaka (striding); ugra (ferocious); varada (boon-giving); Lakṣmīnarasiṁha (in the company of लक्ष्मी); योगानरसिṁह (seated in योग); girija (emerging from a cave in a mountain) and so on.
The hands of the image may be two or four. In the latter case, the two back-hands hold the शङ्ख (conch) and चक्र (discus), the other two being shown in the act of killing the demon हिरण्यकशिपु. An entire Upaniṣad—the Nṛsiṁhatāpinī, in two parts—is devoted to his worship and meditation.
There are several authors of धर्म-śāstra literature by this name, but not much is known of them.
Some of them are: नरसिṁह, the author of Āpastamba-gṛhyasūtra-kārikā-vṛtti (A. D. 1614); Narasiṁhadeva, author of Durgābhaktitaraṅgiṇī (A. D. 1425-50); नरसिṁह Vājapeyin, author of Nityācāra-pradīpa and नरसिṁह Somayājin, author of Viṣṇupratiṣṭhāvidhidarpaṇa.
Many of these works are still in the manuscript form and not printed.

Nārāyaṇa Guru
(A. D. 1854-1928)
------------------------------------------
If a lotus plant that grows in quagmire can bring out a beautiful blossom which is also fragrant, there is no reason why a great man should not be born in a family belonging to a socially berated caste. This is exactly what the highly venerated नारायण गुरु has shown to the world.

D. 1854. His parents were Mādan and Kuṭṭi Amma. They belonged to the ezhava caste (caste of the toddy-tappers, considered untouchables). Being very intelligent he managed to get a good एदुचतिओन् especially from a great teacher Rāman Piḷḷai Āsan of Karunāgapalli village.
Though married as per the usual social customs, the death of his wife soon after, made him roam about like a mendicant. He met two great teachers—Kuñjan Piḷḷai (Ceṭṭāmbi Svāmi) and Thīkkāḍu Ayyāvu—who helped him to attain scholarship and proficiency in योग.
Later, he settled down in a forest near the town Aruvīpuram and practised meditation and austerities. Attaining great inner peace and realising the mission of his life, he established an आश्रम (monastery) there itself and started several social service activities.
His pure life and universal love transcending all social barriers attracted a large number of persons who became his disciples and followers. He also started building temples of शिव and training the priests to worship there.
Thus नारायण became नारायण गुरु by his life and work.
He specially crusaded against इग्नोरन्चे and superstition, untouchability, drinking, animal sacrifice as also cruelty to animals, caste-animosities and a host of other unhealthy practices prevalent in the society.
Attracted by his personality and teachings many young persons joined him, forming an organisation now known as Śrī Nārāyaṇaguru धर्म Paripālana Yogam (S. N. D. P. Yogam).
Nārāyaṇa गुरु established in A. D. 1904 a Gurukulāśrama at Śivagiri 48 kms. (30 miles) to the north of Tiruvanantha-puram where poor children, irrespective of their caste were given good एदुचतिओन्, including vocational training. He also started many more schools of Sanskrit and English, as also an Advaitāśrama at Āḷvāy to teach universal brotherhood.
He took active part in what is now known as Vaikom Satyāgraha, to gain entry into the हिन्दु तेम्प्लेस् for the untouchable castes.
He has written quite a few books in Malayāḷam (his मोथेर्-tongue) and Sanskrit, of which Brahmavidyāpañcakam and Darśanamālā are well-known.

Narahari Tīrtha
(A. D. 1250-1335)
------------------------------------------
Among the four chief disciples of मध्वाचार्य (A. D. 1238-1317), नरहरि तीर्थ was the third. Known as Svāmi-śāstri in his premonastic days, he was an officer of the kings of कलिङ्ग (Orissa) of the Gajapati Dynasty. When मध्वाचार्य visited the kingdom, it was Svāmiśāstri—being the most learned among the court pundits—who had to face him in philosoph-ical disputation. Being vanquished by him, Svāmiśāstri, as per the original covenant, renounced the world and became a saṁ-nyāsin-disciple of मध्वाचार्य, assuming the monastic name ‘Narahari Tīrtha.’
He stayed back in his place, obeying the injunctions of his गुरु. When the royal dynasty was about to collapse due to the death of the young king and the kingdom plunge into chaos, he assumed the reins of the king and ruled very efficiently until the heir-apparent came of age, to take over.
As per the desire of मध्वाचार्य, he secured the beautiful images of सीता and राम from the new king and returned to उडुपि to join his preceptor. It is said that मध्वाचार्य worshipped the images for 80 days and then bequeathed the same to Padmanābha Tīrtha, the first of the four disciples. नरहरि तीर्थ became the abbot after the demise of Padmanābha Tīrtha, in A. D. 1324.
Narahari Tīrtha was a great scholar in Sanskrit and द्वैत Vedānta as also a poet in Kannada language. His songs in Kannada have the aṅkita (assumed title) ‘Raghupati,’ though, sometimes, he has used his real name itself (‘Nṛhari,’ ‘Narahari’). He wrote a ṭippaṇī (brief notes) on the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya of मध्वाचार्य. He is reputed to have written an independent commentary on the Bhagavadgītā. Some of the other works referred to by other writers as his, are: Karmanirṇaya, Tattvadyota and Khaṇḍanatraya.

nara
------------------------------------------
A human being is called ‘nara’ since he is led into this world by his कर्म (deserts of actions) done in the previous lives (nṛ naye = to lead).
Nara is also the name of Lord विष्णु (vide Viṣṇusahasranāma, no. 246). It is interpreted as:
One who inspires a human being into actions and also gives the fruits of the same;
One who is beyond death and destruction (ra = kṣaya or destruction; na = not).
One who is changeless;
One who destroys the miseries of human beings.
See also NARA-NĀRĀYAṆA.

Narasiṁhapurāṇa
------------------------------------------
Hindu mythological literature, through the पुराणस्, the उपपुराणस् and allied works, has successfully kept up the fire and spirit of हिन्दुइस्म् in the hearts of its adherents.
Among the उपपुराणस्, the Nara-siṁhapurāṇa—also spelt as Nṛsiṁha-purāṇa—is considered not only as a fairly ancient one but also important, especially from the standpoint of the Pāñcarātra school of the भागवत cult.
The original purāṇa is supposed to have had 18,000 verses, though the present printed version contains only 3400 verses spread over 68 chapters. It is quite likely that the original might have been lost and later compilers might have redacted it from the available material since many of its verses have been quoted by several writers of धर्मशास्त्रस्. The extant edition might be assigned to the period A. D. 900, though some scholars push it back to A. D. 400-500.
This purāṇa, as its very name suggests, glorifies नरसिṁह as a form of विष्णु. He is identical with नारायण, the eternal ब्रह्मन्.
Apart from the usual topics commonly dealt with in the पुराणस्, it also deals with the practice of योग, worship of नरसिṁह, genealogical lists of kings and some stories like the birth of अश्विनी-kumāras. The chapters 57 to 61 are found to appear as an independent work bearing the title Hārītasaṁhitā or Laghuhārīta-smṛti.

naraka
(‘a world which is below;’ ‘a world without joy’)
------------------------------------------
It may appear strange—but it is true —that the humankind has, throughout its chequered history on this planet of ours, believed in a Super Power (call it ‘God’ if you like) that rewards the good and punishes the wicked. The good are those that faithfully follow the Law as given in the Scriptures whereas the wicked are the transgressors. If the good go to हेअवेन् to enjoy the fruits of their good deeds, the wicked go to हेल्ल् to pay through their nose, for all their heinous crimes, by intense suffering.
In the Ṛgveda (10.14.2) यम and वरुण are mentioned as the deities supervising over the destinies of human beings after death.
The concepts of स्वर्ग (heaven) and नरक (hell) are often found in the उपनिषद्स्. For instance, स्वर्ग or स्वर्ग-लोक is mentioned in the following उपनिषद्स्: Aitareya 4.6; Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.8; Chāndogya 3.13.6; Kaṭha 1.12.
Of course, here, ‘svarga’ may not mean only a हेअवेन् from where there is a fall after exhausting religious merit. It may, sometimes, mean लिबेरतिओन् also as in Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.8.
The word ‘naraka’ has been defined as ‘going below’ or ‘a place where there is not the slightest trace of joy’.
The Nirukta (See NIRUKTA.) quotes a part of a verse from the Ṛgveda (khila) (10.106.1) wherein the word ‘naraka’ is mentioned. By the time of the smṛtis and धर्मशास्त्रस् the concept was fairly well-developed.
By summing up the various ideas about नरक or हेल्ल्, it can be said that यम (the god of death) rules from his capital city called ‘Saṁyamanī’ which is grand and beautiful. A part of his capital houses the various narakas (torture-chambers?) to where the condemned sinners are sent.
The number of narakas ranges from seven to twenty-one. Later पुराणस् have raised this number to 140 or even more!
Some of the narakas are: Andhatā-misra (blinding darkness); Tāmisra (darkness); रौरव (abounding in paths with heated surfaces); Mahāvīcī (where one is submerged in surging waves); Tapana (as hot as fire); Kākola (where one is preyed upon by crows); Lohaśaṅku (piercing one with iron nails); Asipatravana (where one is cut up by many sword blades) and Kumbhīpāka (putting the sinners into big pots of boiling oil).
Special bodies are provided to the sinners (after death here) in narakas, which cause terrible suffering but do not get destroyed!
See also PĀTĀLA and SVARGA.

Nārāyaṇasūkta
(‘hymn to नारायण’)
------------------------------------------
The Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad forms the fourth section of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka. It is often considered as खिल or supplement to the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, which precedes it. It contains four well-known Vedic sūktas, of which the Nārāyaṇasūkta is the most important. It forms the thirteenth अनुवाक or section and has twelve mantras or stanzas. It is generally used to offer flowers at the end of a पूजा (ritualistic worship) or even chanted on auspicious occasions.
It describes the greatness of Nārā-yaṇa, the Supreme God and how to meditate on him in one’s heart.
A general translation of the same, verse by verse, is as follows:
Verse 1
This universe is truly the Divine Person only. Therefore it subsists on him. He, the Divine Being, has countless heads and eyes. He is the giver of joy to the universe. It is He who exists in the form of the universe and is also the abode of all the human beings. He is self-effulgent, imperishable and the final abode of all.
Verse 2
He has transcended the universe. He is eternal. He is all-pervading, refuge of all humanity and the destroyer of sins. This universe is verily that Divine Person and on Him it subsists.
Verse 3
He is the lord of this universe. He is the Self of all beings as also the ruler. He is eternal, indestructible and ever auspicious. He has entered into all beings as the in-dweller. He is supremely worthy of being known (or realised). Though embodied in the universe (as its original cause) he is also the goal of all, the highest refuge.
Verse 4
Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Reality designated as ब्रह्मन्. He is the highest (Self). He is the Supreme Light. He is the infinite Self. He is the excellent meditator and meditation.
Verse 5
Whatever there is in this world, directly perceived or known through the scriptures, नारायण has pervaded all that, both within and without.
Verse 6
One should meditate upon the Supreme, dwelling in the heart, who is limitless, unchanging, omniscient, the giver of happiness to all, as the goal of all striving. The place of His meditation is the ether in the heart which is like an inverted lotus-bud.
Verse 7
It should be known that the heart which is located at the distance of a finger-span below the Adam’s apple, and above the navel is the great abode of the universe and, which is shining like a garland of flames.
Verse 8
Like the bud of a lotus, the heart is suspended in an inverted position, surrounded by arteries. In it or near it, there is a narrow space (called सुषुम्ना). In it everything is supported.
Verse 9
In the middle of that (suṣumnā) remains the undecaying, all-knowing, omnifaced, great fire which has flames on every side. It enjoys the ड़ोओद् presented before it and assimilates it. Its rays are scattered vertically and horizontally.
Verse 10
It warms its own body from the foot to the head. In the centre of that fire there abides a tongue of fire which is extremely fine (or subtle).
Verse 11
It is dazzling like the flash of the lightning that appears in the middle of a rain-bearing cloud, which is slender as the awn of a paddy grain and which serves as a simile to illustrate subtlety.
Verse 12
Paramātman (Supreme Self) dwells in the middle of that flame. It is He who has become ब्रह्मा, शिव, इन्द्र and the अक्षर (Imperishable). It is He who is the Supreme Ruler.
In some texts there are two additional stanzas:
He is Ṛta (the Cosmic Law), सत्य (the Truth), the highest ब्रह्मन्, the dark and tawny Person who has absolute control over Himself. He has strange and variegated eyes and is omniform. We meditate on Him and bow down to Him.
This is the famous Nārāyaṇa gāyatrī: ‘We know नारायण. We meditate on वासुदेव. May that विष्णु inspire us!’
In sum, we can say that this is an excellent hymn, not only for prayer but also for meditation.

Nārada-परिव्राजक-Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
INTRODUCTION
Though classed among the minor उपनिषद्स्, the Nāradaparivrājaka Upaniṣad—assigned to the Atharva Veda —is a fairly big work dealing exclusively with सṁन्यास or pārivrājya (monastic life). It is one of the seventeen such works.
There is only one Sanskrit commentary, by Upaniṣad-brahmayogin.
It is divided into nine ‘upadeśas’ or chapters containing the teaching. These upadeśas comprise both verses in the anuṣṭubh metre and sections in prose, the total being 298.
A brief summary of the text may now be attempted here.
First Chapter
The Upaniṣad begins with the sages शौनक and others approaching the देवर्षि (divine-sage) नारद and requesting him to explain the means to मुक्ति or salvation. In reply नारद states that it is the परमहṁस-saṁnyāsin—the monk of the highest order—who is constantly meditating on his own Self, that attains salvation. However, before attaining this status, he has to undergo several preliminary disciplines that include the study of the वेदस् and other branches of learning form a competent teacher, मर्रिअगे and duly discharging the duties of the householder’s life, acquiring the four means of spiritual life (= साधनचतुष्टय), renouncing the world and taking to the life of the saṁnyāsin.
Second Chapter
Then the sages ask him about the formalities and procedure needed in adopting सṁन्यास. Thinking that it is best to get the answer to this query from ब्रह्मा (the four-faced creator of the world) himself, नारद takes all these sages to सत्यलोक (the abode of ब्रह्मा). After respectfully offering salutations to him, नारद requests him to explain the true nature of pārivrājya or सṁन्यास.
In reply, ब्रह्मा states that a person should first undergo the उपनयन ceremony and study the वेदस् as also acquire the knowledge of other sciences needed to live in the world, for twelve years. For the next twenty five years, he should live as a householder discharging all the duties of that life. The subsequent twenty five years should be spent as a वानप्रस्थ with all the disciplines associated with it. Then he should renounce everything and go away as a mendicant, burning up of all desires and cultivating the four-fold discipline of Vedānta being the precondition to this stage of life. (See SĀDHANA-CATUṢṬAYA.)
Third Chapter
In answer to the question by नारद, as to who is fit to be initiated into सṁन्यास, ब्रह्मा first rules out the following persons as unfit even though they may be endowed with the spirit of renunciation: eunuchs, sinners, physically disabled persons, libertines, children, those who do not accept the authority of the वेदस् and so on.
Then he mentions that a person who is about to die (= ātura) can take सṁन्यास if he has a strong desire, just by uttering the praiṣamantra (oṁ bhūḥ saṁnyastam mayā etc.). In his case there is no need for the performance of the usual rites associated with it.
After declaring that only the person fired with the spirit of intense renunciation is fit for सṁन्यास, he goes on to narrate vidvat-सṁन्यास (saṁnyāsa taken by a man of spiritual illumination).
A person of spiritual illumination generally has the following characteristics: knowledge of ब्रह्मन्; desirelessness and detachment; equanimity under all circumstances; internal and external purity; peace of मिन्द्; devotion to truth; contentment; absence of greed and hypocrisy; sinlessness.
Such a person is eminently fitted to become a vidvat-saṁnyāsin.
He is expected to possess only a minimum number of articles like kaupīna (loin cloth), kanthā (cotton-rug made of cloth-pieces), दण्ड (staff) and कमण्डलु (waterpot) needed for the maintenance of the body. He should always move about all alone. Violation of these rules will cast him into हेल्ल्.
Next, a strict code of conduct is prescribed for the यति or the monk. Some of them are: eschewing the ariṣaḍvargas (the six enemies like lust, anger and so on); conquest of the senses; control of speech and मिन्द्; avoiding honour and welcoming dishonour by the society; forbearance; taking delight in the Self; studying the उपनिषद्स् and allied works; constant effort to conquer all attachment to the physical body; living alone under trees and deserted places; not mixing with others or talking to them about worldly matters: avoiding tasty ड़ोओद्.
Pārivrājya or सṁन्यास can be resorted to in the usual order of the four āśramas—brahmacarya, गार्हस्थ्य, vāna-prastha and saṁnyāsa—or from any stage, intense spirit of renunciation being the only criterion.
Now, नारद asks ब्रह्मा whether the saṁnyāsin who has no śikhā (tuft of hair) and यज्ञोपवीत is a ब्राह्मण at all, since they are essential for him. ब्रह्मा replies that for such a saṁnyāsin, ब्रह्मन् (the Absolute) (or the constant experience of ब्रह्मन्) is everything, including all these insignias of a ब्राह्मण.
The last part describes the state of an अवधूत (the highest saṁnyāsin who has shaken off all bonds and bondages) in a vivid manner. Much of this description is a repetition of the earlier statements. The sages who had attained this state are also mentioned. They are: श्वेतकेतु, Ṛbhu, Nidāgha, ऋषभ, Durvāsa, Saṁvartaka, दत्तात्रेय and Raivataka.
Fourth Chapter
This chapter deals with three topics: the detailed code of conduct prescribed for a normal saṁnyāsin; rites connected with taking formal सṁन्यास; and, some more details regarding the vidvat-saṁnyāsin and the vividiṣā-saṁnyāsin (one who takes सṁन्यास as a mode of sādhanā for मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्).
Some of the steps involved in taking kramasaṁnyāsa—saṁnyāsa in the usual order of the four āśramas—are as follows: prāyaścittas (expiations for sins that might have been committed unknowingly); śrāddhas (ceremonies for satisfying the gods, sages, manes and others); shaving the head and the face; सन्ध्या ritual and Gāyatrījapa (1000 times); final offerings into the Vedic fires if they had been maintained; disposing off the Vedic fires after performing विरजाहोम (a special fire ritual, obligatory for those taking सṁन्यास); uttering the praiṣamantra (signifying total renunciation, using the व्याहृतिस् of Gāyatrīmantra); giving up the śikhā (tuft of hair) and the यज्ञोपवीत (sacred thread); approaching the गुरु and receiving the gerua cloth as also the mahā-vākya (See MAHĀVĀKYAS.); retiring from the world and going away as a mendicant.
This is followed by a short description of the vidvatsaṁnyāsin, who approaches a गुरु, receives the प्रणव (Om) and the mahāvākya. Then he goes about completely naked, sustaining the body only on fruits and water, ever enjoying the bliss of the आत्मन् in his heart.
As regards the vividiṣāsaṁnyāsin, more details are provided as to how he has to formally accept it. Some of them are: approaching a competent गुरु for सṁन्यास; receiving the various articles of सṁन्यास like दण्ड (tall staff), kaupīna (loin cloth), śāṭī (covering cloth) and कमण्डलु (waterpot).
They should be received with appropriate Vedic mantras. Then he should live his life as a saṁnyāsin as per the rules given in the धर्मशास्त्रस्.
Fifth Chapter
In reply to further questioning by नारद, सṁन्यास of four types is described by the Pitāmaha. They are: वैराग्य-सṁन्यास, jñānasaṁnyāsa, jñānavairāgya-सṁन्यास and कर्म-सṁन्यास.
One who renounces the world due to वैराग्य (intense spirit of renunciation) brought about by the पुण्य or the spiritual merit of previous lives is a वैराग्य-saṁnyāsin.
If a person embraces सṁन्यास after realising ( = ज्ञान or knowledge) the true nature of the world and worldly life (as evanescent) he is called a jñānasaṁnyāsin.
When a combination of these two, brought about by the experiences of the first three āśramas, induces the person to take to सṁन्यास, he is a ज्ञान-वैराग्य-saṁnyāsin.
One who accepts the fourth आश्रम (= सṁन्यास) as a matter of course, even though there is no वैराग्य, is known as a karmasaṁnyāsin.
This is then followed by a classification of the saṁnyāsins into six varieties. They are: कुटीचक, बहूदक, हṁस, parama-हṁस, turīyātīta and अवधूत.
The kutīcaka has the śikhā and the यज्ञोपवीत intact. The दण्ड (staff) and कमण्डलु (waterpot) are the insignia he keeps. Kaupīna (loin-cloth) and kanthā (rug) are his possessions. He serves his parents and teachers. He takes his ड़ोओद् from one and the same place (usually his own होउसे). He also wears the religious marks (puṇḍra) on his forehead.
The बहूदक has all the characteristics of the कुटीचक, the only difference being that he begs his ड़ोओद् from a number of houses—this is called mādhukarī—instead of always taking it from one होउसे.
The हṁस has matted hair, applies त्रिपुण्ड्र (religious mark) on his forehead, wears only a kaupīna and gets his भिक्षा or alms from wherever it is got.
The परमहṁस does not keep the śikhā and the यज्ञोपवीत, wears only a kaupīna, a śāṭī (upper cloth) and a दण्ड, applies भस्म or sacred ash all over his body, begs for ड़ोओद् from a maximum of five houses (and that too at night only), eats from his cupped hands (without using any vessel), and practises intense renunciation.
The turīyātīta is naked, lives on any ड़ोओद् got without asking, or, may beg from three houses and treats his body as if it is a corpse, since he is not conscious of it.
The अवधूत, being above all rules and regulations, maintains his body by alms from anyone who cares to give and is always immersed in his own आत्मन् or the Self.
If a person on the verge of (imminent) death takes āturasaṁnyāsa but survives later, he has to take formal सṁन्यास in the usual, traditional way.
Pitāmaha (Brahmā) then goes on to describe the procedural details of taking सṁन्यास by these six kinds of अस्चेतिच्स्.
Other topics touched upon in this section are: modes of accepting भिक्षा; worlds attained by these अस्चेतिच्स् after death; meditation on ब्रह्मन्; evil effects of failure to observe the monastic disciplines; rules concerning begging for ड़ोओद् and living places; details of conduct concerning self-control; giving up all actions save those needed for maintaining the body alive; extreme forbearance; and, trying to see God in all beings.
Sixth Chapter
Nārada now asks ब्रह्मा how the vidvatsaṁnyāsin, who is constantly meditating on his own essential nature (as आत्मन्), becomes liberated. What is the उपाय or the means he adopts?
In answer, ब्रह्मा states, in a highly symbolical language, how the vidvat-saṁnyāsin looks upon his own body. For instance, ज्ञान (knowledge) is his body. वैराग्य (renunciation) is the life-force. Śānti (peace) and dānti (self control) are his eyes. मनस् (mind is his face and so on.
Incidentally, how the जीव (the individual सोउल्) moves about in the various petals of the heart (the अनाहतचक्र) and the results he experiences are also described.
How to attain the turīyātīta state (the state beyond the fourth, of the jīvātman or the individual सोउल्) is the subject-matter of the next section. The जप of the haṁsamantra (See BRAHMA-विद्या UPANIṢAD and HAṀSA.) will ultimately lead to it. Being bereft of body-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् he becomes ब्रह्मन्.
Then comes a long description of the way, a saṁnyāsin should live, not violating the norms of धर्म (even though he may be a jīvanmukta), to set an example before the world. Some of the rules mentioned here are: conquest of all sense-organs; light ड़ोओद्; constant meditation on ब्रह्मन्; not taking part in rituals; going for alms to the houses after the members of the family have finished their ड़ोओद् and so on.
However, it is also stated that such a vidvatsaṁnyāsin is beyond the realms of वर्ण and आश्रम, and hence known as ‘ativarṇāśramin’.
This is followed once again, by the rules an aspirant for सṁन्यास and मोक्ष (a vividiṣāsaṁnyāsin) is expected to follow. Preliminary disciplines to be practised, approaching a competent गुरु (teacher) and sincerely serving him for at least a year, after which formal vows of सṁन्यास may be taken from him are also described. Some more general rules of conduct, applicable to him, are given once again. The gist of these is self-control and renunciation of all actions.
Seventh Chapter
Being asked by नारद once again about the rules a यति (saṁnyāsin) has to follow in his life, Pitāmaha expatiates on it. Summarised briefly the rules are as follows: itinerant way of life for eight months and staying in one place for four months during the rainy season, but always alone; avoiding all actions that may harm other living beings; accepting very simple ड़ोओद् as alms, just to sustain the body; eschewing all items of luxury as poison; shunning the places and persons connected with the earlier (pre-monastic) life; burning up the six passions (See ARIṢAḌVARGA.); trying to see or visualise his own आत्मन् (the Self) in everyone and everything; meditating on his own आत्मन् or Self always, until the body falls after the exhaustion of प्रारब्धकर्म.
In the next ten paragraphs, some more directions regarding the life-style of the six kinds of मोन्क्स् already mentioned, are dealt with. They are: स्नान (bath); पुण्ड्र (wearing of religious marks); kṣaura (shaving the head and beard); अन्न (food); śāṭī (covering cloth); religious rites like arcana (worship); mantrajapa (repetition of divine names or Vedic passages); repeating the प्रणव (Om); śravaṇa, मनन and निदिध्यासन (hearing, reflecting and meditating).
Eighth Chapter
Nārada requests ब्रह्मा to enlighten him about the saṁsāratāraka, the मन्त्र that takes one across the ocean of transmigratory existence. Consenting to do so. ब्रह्मा talks in detail on the प्रणव or ओङ्कार in all its aspects. Eight forms of प्रणव such as Antaḥpraṇava, Vyāvahārikapraṇava, Ārṣapraṇava and so on, are described in great detail.
This is then followed by a method of meditation on ब्रह्मन् who is sarvādhāra (support of all), jyoti (light), sarveśvara (lord of all), personification of all gods and scriptures.
The section ends with the description of the four states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and the आत्मन् associated with them, as found in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad.
Ninth Chapter
This chapter describes the nature of ब्रह्मन्, quoting verses from some of the major उपनिषद्स्, followed by the eulogy of realising it. It is also declared that only a person of the highest moral calibre can realise it.
One who knows ब्रह्मन् as described here, will be liberated (soon after the body falls).
The last part describes once again the parivrāḍ (= saṁnyāsin) who is a jīvan-mukta (liberated even while living) and that he does not return to mundane existence again.
EPILOGUE
This is an important Upaniṣad dealing with सṁन्यास exhaustively and is almost like a textbook for the saṁnyāsins.

Nārāyaṇīya
(‘pertaining to नारायण’)
------------------------------------------
The devotional cults of हिन्दुइस्म् have been divided into two main streams: the Śaiva (that of शिव; this includes the शाक्त or the cult of the Divine मोथेर्) and the Vaiṣṇava (that of विष्णु), (also known as the भागवत cult).
One of the basic and very important texts—perhaps the oldest too—is the Nārāyaṇīya section of the Mahābhārata, comprising the 18 chapters (chs. 334 to 351) of the Śāntiparva (the 12th book of the epic). The total number of verses—which sometimes includes paragraphs and sentences in prose also—is 1310.
The entire section is devoted to the glorification of Lord नारायण, his devotees, and the nature of devotion to be cultivated towards him.
A brief summary of this section may now be attempted here:
Chapter 1 (Ch. 334; 45 verses)
Nārada visits the बदरिकाश्रम where नर and नारायण (the twin sages) are performing severe austerities. In reply to नारद’s question as to whom he was meditating upon and worshipping, the sage नारायण replies that it was on the Supreme God (Nārāyaṇa).
Chapter 2 (Ch. 335; 55 verses)
As per the directions of the sage नारायण, नारद visits the श्वेतद्वीप, the island beyond the mountain मेरु. He is wonder-struck to see there, the multitude of devotees of Lord नारायण, who were absolutely white in colour (śveta = white) and were deeply immersed in meditation on him.
Chapter 3 (Ch. 336; 65 verses)
The great sacrifice performed by the king Uparicara—a devotee of the highest order—under the guidance of the sage बृहस्पति forms the subject matter of this chapter.
Chapter 4 (Ch. 337; 41 verses)
This chapter describes how the king Uparicara, though he had attained हेअवेन्, fell from there since he permitted the immolation of a goat in a sacrifice, thereby committing हिṁसा (violence). He was however saved by the Lord नारायण by the power of the अष्टाक्षरी (eight-lettered) मन्त्र (= oṁ namo nārāyaṇāya) which he was constantly repeating.
Chapter 5 (Ch. 338; 200 names of the Lord)
This chapter contains a long hymn in prose, in praise of Lord नारायण, by the sage नारद while in the श्वेतद्वीप. It has 200 epithets.
Chapter 6 (Ch. 339; 141 verses)
Pleased by नारद’s devotional prayer, the Lord नारायण appears before him in his Cosmic Form (Viśvarūpa) which was indescribably beautiful and brilliant.
Nārada is advised by the Lord to serve the sages नर and नारायण of the बदरिकाश्रम.
There is also a brief description of the four व्यूहस्: वासुदेव, सङ्कर्षण, प्रद्युम्न and अनिरुद्ध. (See CATUR-VYŪHAS for details.)
Chapter 7 (Ch. 340; 119 verses)
This chapter is mainly devoted to the delineation of pravṛttidharma (performance of one’s duties as prescribed by the śāstras or scriptures), yajñas or वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् being the main part of the same. Towards the end, nivṛttidharma (path of knowledge and renunciation) is also touched upon.
Chapter 8 (Ch. 341; 51 verses)
The various names by which Lord कृष्ण was praised are described here along with their etymological meanings by कृष्ण himself to अर्जुन. The identity of ब्रह्मा and रुद्र (Śiva) with नारायण (or कृष्ण) has also been stressed.
Chapter 9 (Ch. 342; 142 verses including prose paras)
This section is a combination of verses interspersed with prose passages. It des-cribes सृष्टि or च्रेअतिओन्, greatness of ब्राह्मणस् (the wise spiritual persons), story of the sage दधीचि (See DADHĪCI.), story of the king नहुष being cursed by the sage अगस्त्य, च्रेअतिओन् of the work Nirukta by the sage यास्क, about the four वेदस् and fighting between रुद्र and नारायण.
Chapter 10 (Ch. 343; 66 verses)
In this chapter, the second visit of the sage नारद to श्वेतद्वीप and revisiting the sages नर and नारायण are described.
Chapter 11 (Ch. 344; 27 verses)
This short section expounds the nature of Lord वासुदेव, the highest aspect of नारायण.
Chapter 12 (Ch. 345; 28 verses)
The origin of śrāddha and तर्पण (obsequial rites), attributed to the वराहावतार (boar-इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु) is expounded here.
Chapter 13 (Ch. 346; 22 verses)
This chapter is a eulogy of the merit one gets by listening to the greatness of Lord नारायण.
Chapter 14 (Ch. 347; 96 verses)
When the two demons मधु and कैटभ had stolen the वेदस्, विष्णु took the form of हयग्रीव (See HAYAGRĪVA for details.) and recovered them. Later on he killed the demons also. This is the gist of the contents of this chapter.
Chapter 15 (Ch. 348; 88 verses)
This chapter describes how the Sātvatadharma (or Bhāgavatadharma, religion of devotion towards Lord नारायण or विष्णु) was taught by the Lord, but, forgotten again and again by the receivers. To receive it and propagate it in the world, ब्रह्मा had to take seven births! This धर्म of single-minded devotion taught in the उपनिषद्स् and the Pāñcarātra Āgamas is superior to the path of ज्ञान (knowledge) and can be got only by God’s grace.
Chapter 16 (Ch. 349; 74 verses)
The birth of the sage व्यास, first as the sage Apāntaratamas and later as कृष्ण-द्वैपायन, is described here. How he edited and divided the वेदस् as also his encyclopedic knowledge are also delineated. Another interesting point stressed here is that all the five well-known philosophies contained in the metaphysical systems of Sāṇkhya, योग, Pāñcarātra, वेदस् and पाशुपत lead to the same goal viz., नारायण!
Chapter 17 (Ch. 350; 27 verses)
This is a short chapter describing the meeting between ब्रह्मा the creator, and शिव, represented here as his son. The ensuing conversation is continued in detail in the next chapter.
Chapter 18 (Ch. 351; 23 verses)
This is also a short chapter.
It gives a beautiful description of Lord नारायण, not only in the cosmic aspect—reminiscent of the one given in the Puruṣasūkta (Ṛgveda 10.7.90)—but also as the अन्तर्यामिन् (inner controller). The four व्यूहस् are also referred to.
It is thus seen that this Nārāyaṇīya section of the Mahābhārata is specially devoted—as its very name indicates—to the exposition of the glory of Lord नारायण.
Nārāyaṇīyam is also the name of an extremely elegant poetical work on the कृष्ण-theme, characterised by literary grace and devotional fervour. नारायण भट्टातिरि (A. D. 1560-1625) of Meppattūr in the Kerala State is its illustrious author. (See NĀRĀYAṆA BHAṬṬĀTIRI for details.)
This work is a faithful poetical condensation of the entire Bhāgavata. It is in one hundred daśakas (decades or cantos of ten stanzas), the total number of verses —which are in various meters—being a little more than one thousand (1036, to be exact).

Nāradīya-purāṇa
------------------------------------------
Though the Hindu पुराणस् are sometimes described as ‘Cock-and-bull-stories’, their main purpose is to inform and inspire the common masses to better and ethically purer ways of life, both at the personal and at the social levels.
There are two purāṇas—both belonging to the Upapurāṇa group—attributed to the divine sage नारद: The Bṛhan-nāradīyapurāṇa and the Nāradīyapurāṇa (also spelt as Nāradapurāṇa).
The Nāradīyapurāṇa as available now, may not be the same as the one referred to in the Matsya, the Skanda or the Agni पुराणस्. Scholars generally assign it to the period A. D. 700-1000. The first part (pūrvabhāga) has 125 chapters in four pādas or quarters. The second part (uttarabhāga) has 82 chapters.
The first part is sometimes identified with the Bṛhan-nāradīya-purāṇa.
The contents in brief are as follows: praise of विष्णु, and भक्ति or devotion; geography of भारतवर्ष (India); story of भगीरथ bringing the गङ्गा river from हेअवेन् and its greatness; a few vratas; varṇāśramadharmas; pātakas or sins; सदाचार or good conduct; śrāddha or obsequial ceremonies.
The story of the king रुक्माङ्गद who was a great devotee of विष्णु and who meticulously observed the एकादशी vrata has received a detailed treatment. (See RUKMĀṄGADA for details.)
See also BṚHAN-NĀRADĪYA-PURĀṆA.

Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a short Upaniṣad classed among the Minor उपनिषद्स् of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. It has four khaṇḍas or sections, all in prose.
The first describes how नारायण, the पुरुष (Paramapuruṣa, the Supreme Person) desired to create the world of beings. From him evolved the following objects and beings: प्राण (the vital force); मनस् (mind); इन्द्रियस् (the ten sense-organs); the पञ्चभूतस् (five elements); the gods ब्रह्मा, रुद्र and इन्द्र; the nine Prajāpatis (like दक्ष); the twelve Ādityas, the eleven Rudras and the eight वसुस्; and, lastly, all the वेदस्. All these get manifested out of नारायण, are activated by him during the life of the created world, and then, get merged back in him at the end of the cycle.
The second khaṇḍa describes how नारायण is eternal and how ब्रह्मा, शिव, इन्द्र, time in its three aspects, the quarters, and all the directions are all different facets of नारायण. नारायण who is without parts, without any imperfections or changes or names, is absolutely pure and the one without a second. One who knows him thus, becomes विष्णु Himself.
The third khaṇḍa describes the well-known aṣṭākṣarīmantra, the मन्त्र of eight letters of Nārāyaṇa—oṁ namo nārāyaṇāya. One who repeats this great मन्त्र regularly as per the directions of the गुरु (spiritual teacher), will transcend all dishonour and will live long. He will also get wealth, cows and other objects of desire while living here and go to ब्रह्मलोक (the world of ब्रह्मा) after death. Later on, he will attain final लिबेरतिओन्.
The last khaṇḍa describes नारायण as ब्रह्मन्, the पुरुष (the all-pervading Being) who is of the nature of प्रणव (Oṁ) comprising the three syllables a, u and m. The योगि who utters this प्रणव or the aṣṭākṣarīmantra will be liberated from the bondage of सṁसार (transmigration) and attain the world called वैकुण्ठ (the Abode of विष्णु).
This नारायण who is pure solidified चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् resides in the lotus of the heart. He is identified with Devakīputra-कृष्ण, who is dear to the knowers of ब्रह्मन् or to whom the latter are dear. He is also the dweller in the hearts of all beings, the un-caused Cause of the universe.
The Upaniṣad concludes with the eulogy that its study will destroy all sins, will bestow the merit of reciting all the वेदस्, ultimately resulting in merging into नारायण Himself.

Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭātiri
(A. D. 1560-1625)
------------------------------------------
There can perhaps be no better example than that of नारायण भट्टातिरि to prove that a chance utterance from a great सोउल् can lift a person from the ridiculous to the sublime.
Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭātiri is more well-known as the author of the immortal epic poem Nārāyaṇīyam. He was born at Meppattūr (in the Kerala State) in A. D. 1560. His ड़थेर् was Mātṛdatta, an orthodox ब्राह्मण of great erudition, from a famous नम्बूदिरि family.
During his early youth he appeared to be more a profligate than a prodigy which he certainly was. A chance remark of reprobation from Acyuta Piśaraḍī, converted the young नारायण भट्टातिरि into a remorseful but earnest disciple of that great man of profound learning and wisdom.
In course of time, नारायण became a pundit in his own right. When his गुरु fell a victim to paralysis, नारायण, being a devoted disciple, took upon himself that fell disease, thus freeing his master from the same.
However, unable to bear the torments of that disease, he started visiting the temple of Lord कृष्ण at गुरुवायूर् (near Trichur, also in the Kerala State), by being carried to that place. For one hundred days he prayed to the Lord, spontaneously composing 10 verses each day, dealing with the दशावतारस् or ten incarnations of Lord विष्णु. On the last day he was totally freed from that debilitating disease!
This work, now known as the Nārāyaṇīyam, is in ten cantos, the total number of verses being 1036. They are in different meters.
See NĀRĀYAṆĪYAM for details.
Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭātiri was a great scholar in several fields of traditional learning. Eighteen works are attributed to him. Some of them are: Nārāyaṇīyam, Mānameyodaya, Prakriyāsarvasva, Aṣṭamīcampūkāvya, Kailāsaśailavarṇana, Rāmakathā, Rājasūyaprabandha and Ahalyāśāpavimocana.
He had been appointed as the court pundit of the king Devanārāyaṇa of Ambalapura.
He is said to have passed away at the ripe old-age of 106 in A. D. 1666, though some scholars do not subscribe to this view.
A devoted recitation of his Nārāya-ṇīyam is believed to free one from diseases and bestow good health.

Nāradasmṛti
------------------------------------------
Whereas the वेदस् and the Upa-niṣads give the basic ideas of philosophy and, occasionally, some instructions concerning personal एथिच्स् or social conduct, the task of elaborating the latter has been fulfilled admirably by the पुराणस्, smṛtis, धर्मशास्त्रस् and निबन्धस् (digests).
One of the more ancient smṛtis is the Nāradasmṛti. Though नारद is a familiar figure in the mythological literature, the author of this treatise may not be that sage. The work as available now in print comprising 1028 verses has been assigned to the period A. D. 100-300.
There are two commentaries on this work: one by Asahāya (circa A. D. 600-750) which is incomplete and the other by Bhavasvāmin (circa A. D. 700-1000).
Nāradasmṛti follows the Manusmṛti closely. However, it contains greater details and is arranged in a more systematic way.
Some of the subjects dealt with in this work may be listed as follows: ṛṇādāna (recovery of debts); upanidhi (deposits and lending); dattāpradānika (gifts and resumption thereof); abhyupetya-aśuśrūṣā (breach of contract of service); asvāmi-vikraya (sale without ownership); samayasya-anapā-कर्म (violations of the conventions of guilds); sīmābandha (settlement of boundaries); दायभाग (partition and इन्हेरितन्चे); strīpuṁsayoga (marital relations); crimes and punishment. It is seen that almost all these items belong to the field of vyavahāra (social conduct).
Nārada, differing from मनु, allows नियोग (levirate), remarriage of widows and गम्ब्लिन्ग् (but controlled by the State).
Later writers like विश्वरूप (circa A. D. 750-1000), मेधातिथि (A. D. 825-900) and Asahāya have regarded Nāradasmṛti as an authoritative work.

Narsī Mehtā
(A. D. 1415-1481)
------------------------------------------
If Vivekānanda (A. D. 1863-1902) declared that he alone lives who lives for others, he was probably echoing another great saint who preceded him by four centuries, who sang thus: ‘He alone is a Vaiṣṇava—a man of God—who understands the sufferings of others’ (vide his song ‘Vaiṣṇava janato...’). This was नर्सी मेह्ता (also spelt as ‘Narasī Mehatā’), the foremost saint of Gujarat.
Born in A. D. 1415 as the second son of कृष्ण Dāmodar Dās and लक्ष्मी-गौरी (who were नागर-brahmaṇas by caste) at the village Talājā (near the modern town of Junagadh in Gujarat), Narasiṁharām —that was his earlier name—was dumb right from his childhood days. Having lost both the parents at the age of five, he was brought up by his grandmother Jayakuvarī. When he was eight years old, he was suddenly endowed with the power of speech by a great saint, who made him utter the words ‘Rādhā-कृष्ण!’
Narsī MehtāAfter the death of Jayakuvarī, the boy Narsiṁharām or नर्सी मेह्ता, had to be taken care of by his elder brother Vaṁśīdhar and aunt Duritgaurī. As per the traditions of the family, Vaṁśīdhar tried to get him educated and also got him married to Māṇikgaurī, a girl from a good family. Narsī was blessed with two children—a boy and a girl—in course of time. However, this shrew of an aunt made his life so miserable that he, one night, leaving behind his own wife and two children escaped to a deserted temple of Lord शिव on the outskirts of the town.
After seven days of ड़स्तिन्ग् and intense prayer he was blessed with the vision of Lord शिव who was instrumental in vouchsafing to him an actual experience of participating in the रासलीला dance of कृष्ण with the गोपीस्! This changed his whole life permanently and Lord कृष्ण gave him the boon of remaining as his eternal friend, guide and protector.
Narsī Mehtā now started an entirely new life, a life rooted in God, spending most of his time in composing and singing devotional songs related to कृष्ण, as also dancing in ecstasy.
True to his word, as promised in the Bhagavadgītā (9.22), कृष्ण came to the rescue of Narsī many a time, when evil-doers created serious problems. Some of the miraculous happenings described in his traditional biographies are: supplying all the things demanded of Narsī by the parents of his son-in-law; giving plenty of money to a rich man who had brought a ‘demand draft’ issued by Narsī; getting garlanded by कृष्ण himself in the temple, by a garland of तुलसी leaves, and so on.
Narsī’s son predeceased him. This, instead of making him dejected, made him more happy since he could pray to his Lord even more intensely.
He gave up the body in great peace, during the year A. D. 1481.
His contribution to Gujarati literature in the form of beautiful songs of devotion is considerable.
Some of his compositions are: Śyāmaldāsno Vivāh; Hārmālā; Sūrat Saṅgrām; Sudāmācarit; Rāsasahasrapadī; Śṛṅgārmālā; Govindāgaman and Bālalīlā.
He laid great stress on devotion to God and ignored caste restrictions. Cultivation of firm faith in God and dependence on Him are his other teachings.

Nara-Nārāyaṇa
------------------------------------------
After the purpose of नरसिṁह-अवतार was accomplished, नरसिṁह split himself into two, the lion part becoming the sage नारायण and the human part the sage नर. नर and नारायण then retired to बदरिकाश्रम for performing austerities. When इन्द्र tried to seduce them through celestial nymphs, नारायण produced the nymph ऊर्वशी from his thigh (ūru = thigh) who was more beautiful than all of them put together.
