They performed severe austerities and successfully vanquished the demon Sahasrakavaca (one who has a thousand armours).
These sages were reborn later as Śrī कृष्ण and अर्जुन.
This story has an important lesson for us. Every one of us is a mixture of the human and the divine elements. The anti-human and the anti-divine demon is ever attempting to seduce us with his thousand wiles. To successfully vanquish him, we need to perform तपस् or austerity.
Nara-नारायण is represented either as a single person or as two persons. In the former case the icon may have two or four arms carrying the जपमाला (rosary) or the usual emblems of Lord विष्णु. In the latter case, नर may be shown as having two heads and two arms and wearing the deer skin. नारायण is depicted with the usual four arms carrying the emblems शङ्ख, चक्र, पद्म and जपमाला.

Narakāsura
------------------------------------------
He is said to have been born out of a drop of sweat that fell on the earth (or भूदेवी) from the body of Varāha (Boar-इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु). Hence he was known as Bhaumāsura also.
Due to the prayer of भूदेवी, विष्णु gave नरकासुर, the weapon called Vaiṣṇavāstra. Becoming invincible by the possession of this formidable weapon, नरकासुर became a terror to the whole world. He took away the royal umbrella of इन्द्र, the ear-rings of अदिति (Indra’s मोथेर्) as also many other things from हेअवेन्.
When इन्द्र placed his problems before Śrī कृष्ण and begged for his intervention, the latter invaded Prāg-jyotiṣapura, the capital of नरकासुर and killed him as also his chief assistant Murāsura. He then restored all the valuable things that the demon had looted, to their rightful owners.
At the request of Bhūmidevī, he gave protection to Bhagadatta, son of नरकासुर, and crowned him as the king.
The day on which नरकासुर was killed, is observed as the Narakacaturdaśī festival.

Nārada Bhaktisūtras
------------------------------------------
The Nārada Bhaktisūtras is a well-known and popular work on भक्ति or devotion to God. Hence a fairly detailed account may now be given here.
THE IMPORTANCE OF HUMAN BIRTH
We see two classes of things—animate and inanimate—in the Lord’s च्रेअतिओन्. Among the animates there are two classes again—animals and human beings. Only man possesses the intellect and चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् to shape his life and to think independently. That is why Purandara Dāsa (A. D. 1484-1564) said: “Human birth is great, don’t waste it, O crazy men!” It is mentioned in our mythological works that a सोउल् will have passed through eight million and four hundred thousand births before attaining this invaluable human birth!
ENQUIRY FOR TRUTH
After things like ड़ोओद्, clothes and shelter needed for physical sustenance and protection are met, the enquiry for Truth that has been in the heart of every conscious person from the very beginning, gets aroused. Birth and death, natural marvels, the bitter experiences of life—all these make man introspective. “Who am I? What was I before I was born? Where was I? Wherefrom, how and why have I come to this world? What is death? Where do I go after death? Or, is death itself the ultimate state? Do I become extinct then? Where did this world come from? How and why was it created? Who created it? If there is a God who is the creator and ruler of this world, what form has He? What is the relationship between Him and this world, the other living things and my own Self? What is the object of human life? How does one attain it?”—Such questions as these, have been troubling man since time immemorial.
THE VEDAS
Those great men who considered these questions with the seriousness they deserve, dedicating their very lives to find out answers to these questions, discovering solutions to them through austerity, meditation and knowledge, and thereby have become the guiding spirits of later generations, are called ‘ṛṣis’ in this country. The spiritual knowledge that has come down to us from the ṛṣis is called the ‘Vedas’ or ‘Śruti’. We believe that these are not knowledge discovered by the ṛṣis on their own, but are directly revealed in their pure मिन्द् by the Lord Himself. This kind of belief exists in the other important religions of the world too.
VEDĀNTA
The essential aspect of these वेदस् or Śrutis are the उपनिषद्स्. It is customary to call them as ‘Vedānta’. According to this Vedānta, the fundamental reality out of which the world has arisen is ब्रह्मन्, the Ultimate Self. It is real, conscious, infinite and blissful. This च्रेअतिओन् has emerged from It, is supported by It, and gets dissolved in It. We too are the everlasting चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, the Self, which is birthless and deathless that transcends the body, मिन्द् and the senses. The Ultimate Reality is in the heart of this च्रेअतिओन्, as well as ourselves; at the same time, it is beyond all these and exists externally too in its infinite nature. We groan under the revolving wheel of birth and death because of ‘avidyā,’ or इग्नोरन्चे, since we consider that we are the body, the senses and such other things. This is what is called ‘saṁsāra.’ Only when we, the ‘jīvātmas,’ who are in bondage, become aware of ब्रह्मन्, i.e., when we realize It, shall we be free of this wheel of ‘saṁsāra’; we then experience the unceasing, everlasting bliss that is our own. We need to move along the path of truth and righteousness to obtain this freedom. We need to practise control of the senses. We need to love the Ultimate Reality, the Innermost Self.
THE SCHOOLS OF भक्ति-VEDĀNTA
There are differences of approach among various Vedānta traditions about things such as the nature of the Ultimate Reality or the Innermost Self, and, in the same way, the real nature of the jīvātmas, the relationship between the two, the nature of the world, the cause for the bondage of the jīvātmas, their path towards freedom and the state of freedom. Somehow there is a general feeling that ‘Vedānta’ means the non-dual Vedānta of शङ्कर only. This is not correct. Many teachers who came after शङ्कर, and who were great intellectuals, great अस्चेतिच्स्, great seers and great devotees have subjected the Vedānta of शङ्कर to incisive criticism and established their own Vedānta traditions on sound foundations. Among them, the most noteworthy are Rāmānuja (A. D. 1017-1137), Madhva (A. D. 1238-1317), निम्बार्क (12th cent. A. D.), वल्लभ (A. D. 1473-1531) and Śrī कृष्ण चैतन्य (A. D. 1517-1582). The common premise with which they start is that we can attain freedom only through devotion to God and by the grace of God. Hence we can call these schools as ‘The schools of भक्ति Vedānta.’
THE GROWTH OF THE CONCEPT OF BHAKTI
The feeling of devotion to God is very ancient. We see this in many psalms of prayer in the Ṛgveda Saṁhitā itself. For instance—‘He who surrenders himself to विष्णु who is the cause of the world, the ever new, the lord of wealth, he who sings of His sublime birth and actions, he attains विष्णु, who is of the nature of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्.’ (1.156.3)
‘O इन्द्र, you are better than my ड़थेर्, you are greater than my brother who cannot protect me. O Vasu, you and my मोथेर् are the same. Protect me for my wealth.’ (8.1.61)
Though we do not find the term ‘bhakti’ in the ancient उपनिषद्स्, what the term means finds expression in many places. Consider the following मन्त्र found in Kaṭhopaniṣad (2.23) and Muṇḍa-kopaniṣad (3.24):
‘This आत्मन् is not attainable through lectures; He is not attainable through intellect nor through much listening. He whom He chooses, to him alone is (the Self) available. The Self reveals Himself to such a worshipper.’
In another मन्त्र of Kaṭhopaniṣad (2.20) also we see the idea of the grace of God.
Especially in the Śvetāśvataropaniṣad (6.23; 6.18) such terms as भक्ति (devotion) and शरणागति (surrender) are directly used:
‘He who has devotion par excellence to the Lord and devotion of the same kind to the गुरु, to that great man the subjects dealt with here become clear; to that great man (the subjects dealt with here) become clear.’
‘He who created the four-faced ब्रह्मा before the च्रेअतिओन् of the world, and who enlightened him about the वेदस्, He who lights the Self and the intellect, I surrender to Him; I, who desire freedom.’
In this way, many aspects of devotion like love of God, grace of the Lord, devotion to the गुरु and surrender, which appear in their nascent form, grow to great heights by the age of the classics and mythologies. Now, of course, abundant devotional literature is available. A few of the most important works in this field may be mentioned at this point: The Bhagavadgītā of the Mahābhārata (Bhīṣmaparva 25-42) and Nārāyaṇīya (Śāntiparva 322-351), Viṣṇupurāṇa, भागवत, शाण्डिल्य Bhaktisūtras, नारद भक्तिसूत्रस्, Nāradapāñcarātra, अहिर्बुध्न्य सṁहिता, Bhaktirasāyana, Bhaktirasāmṛta Sindhu and so on. Devotional literature is also found extensively in the पुराणस् and the उपपुराणस् also. Additionally, plenty of devotional poems and songs are available in Indian languages.
THE SCHOOL OF BHAKTI
We may now very broadly present the भक्ति School as enunciated in the works of भक्ति Vedānta. The Supreme Self (Paramātman) is without attributes and formless, and at the same time, He has attributes and forms too. These two are the true and equal aspects of the same God; neither of them is superior to the other.
That he has attributes and forms means that he is the great ocean of an infinitude of noble attributes; at the same time, he can manifest himself before his devotees in every form they have adored him (vide Bhagavadgītā 4.11; 7.21). As he is omniscient and omnipotent, this is not impossible for him at all. Sugar dolls are all made of the same material—sugar; in the same way, he is the One Principle that embodies itself into राम, कृष्ण, नारायण, शिव, देवी, गणपति, Subrah-maṇya and a host of other gods and goddesses. He it is who revealed himself to the sages in these various forms and has brought about the system of worship of these gods and goddesses in this world. As the sea is permanently in the form of ice-rocks in the polar regions, it is he himself who resides in the forms of शिव and विष्णु in such worlds as कैलास and वैकुण्ठ. Nothing is impossible for him.
That he is attributeless does not mean that he lacks attributes; it only means that he is one whose greatness is not limited or sullied by his qualities. Or it means that he is not graspable by the three guṇas of nature. Formless means that he has no particular form. As he is within and outside everything, all forms and shapes are his own. As he is of the nature of pure spirit, he can bestow his grace on the worshippers of the attributeless and formless aspect also.
This Supreme Self can incarnate in the form of a human being for the establishment of धर्म (righteousness) in this world (See Bhagavadgītā 4.6-9). Then his body—being unlike our bodies created by कर्म that has already started giving its fruits—is divine, not created by the matrix. He can incarnate even in that small body with his full power; that is why, our worship and adoration of his इन्चर्नतिओन् would be the same as our worship and adoration of him himself (See Chāndogyopaniṣad 6.2.2). The reason for the worldliness or bondage of the jīvātman (the conditioned Self or सोउल्) is due to the fact that he has no devotion to the Supreme Self; because of this, he has been caught in the grip of the power of इल्लुसिओन् (māyā) and suffers in the world (See Śāṇḍilya Bhaktisūtras 98.). Therefore, only through devotion, because of which the Supreme Self showers grace, can the limited Self attain his लिबेरतिओन्. The ज्ञानमार्ग (path of knowledge) which, by means of listening about and reflecting on the Self that is beyond the limitation of the body and the senses, and by deep meditation on that Self, helps attain self-realization and लिबेरतिओन्, is very difficult. The eightfold योग (Rājayoga) which involves control of the मिन्द् and senses also is a hard path. Even the योग of desireless work is also not easy. The योग of devotion, which consists of repetition of God’s name and singing of songs of his adoration, is the very natural and simple path to लिबेरतिओन् in this कलियुग (the Dark Age). This is the stand of the भक्ति Schools.
Everyone is eligible for this path of भक्ति. Caste, community, gender, एदुचतिओन्, innate ability मिन्द्.">1 (saṁskāra)—none of these is an impediment to move along this path (See Śāṇḍilya Bhaktisūtras 78.). गुह, नन्द, Cokkamela, Ravidās, Thiruppāṇāḷvār and कण्णप्प the hunter —these people were untouchables. अजामिल, Ratnākara, Thoṇḍaradippoḍi Āḷvār—these were sinners. शबरी, राधा, Mīrā and Godā were women. कबीर्, Nānak and तुकाराम् had no bookish knowledge. Therefore, what is required is only love for God; this itself will help attain everything.
Bhakti has been defined in various ways in different texts. Nārada Pāñcarātra says that devotion is that love which is directed towards विष्णु alone and has no concern for any other thing. Gopālapūrvatāpanī Upaniṣad mentions that renunciation of this world and the next and total absorption in the Supreme Self indeed is devotion. Bhaktirasāyana on the other hand, defines devotion as the way in which the मिन्द् after getting purified and melted through spiritual practices (sādhanas) flows incessantly towards the Almighty. The Bhāgavata describes the योग of devotion as one in which the मिन्द् flows towards the Lord, as गङ्गा towards the sea, once it hears the attributes of God. The Śāṇḍilya Sūtras states that devotion is intense attachment to the Lord.
Bhakti is divided into different categories in these works: worldly, scriptural (Vedic), and spiritual; physical, vocal and mental; tāmasik, rājasik and sāttvik and so on.
An important characteristic of the practice of devotion is to count the beads according to a discipline, taking the मन्त्र of God given by a worthy गुरु through initiation and keeping in मिन्द् a form of God which is to one’s liking. It need not be emphasized that, as in other kinds of spiritual practices, the following of moral values, the practice of detachment, the company of noble souls and so on, are absolutely essential for this purpose.
These भक्ति scriptures have described the characteristics of a devotee who has realized God. They, to a large extent, resemble the characteristics of the liberated individual described in the Bhagavadgītā (See 2.54-72; 12.13-20; 14.21-26).
NĀRADA BHAKTISŪTRAS
Attention may now be given to the author of this book as well as the work itself.
NĀRADA, THE DIVINE SAGE
Nārada, who is well-known as the divine sage, is a very attractive individual who is well-reputed in our religious literature.
The ṛṣis of the psalm ‘indrasuteṣu someṣu’ in the Ṛgveda Saṁhitā are नारद and कण्व. Again, नारद and Parvata are the ṛṣis to whom the psalms starting with ‘sukhāya ā nivīdata’ have been revealed. We meet नारद, the seer of the mantras, in the Atharvaveda (5.19.9; 12.4.16) too. In the Bhūmavidyā of Chāndogyopaniṣad, नारद is indicated as a disciple of Sanatkumāra. In पुराणस्, of course, he is seen in several places. In the Bhāgavata (1.5, 23-31; 1.6. 5-36), the story of नारद has appeared in a sufficiently detailed fashion. Born as the son of a śūdra maid in the previous life, as a five year old child he served some अस्चेतिच्स् who came to his place for चातुर्मास्य (spending the four months of the rainy season in one place) and was initiated with the Lord’s name through them. On the death of his मोथेर् due to snake bite, he felt sad and wandered about in a forest; there he sat under a tree and had the vision of the Lord Śrīhari in his heart. Then he heard a voice which said to him that, that was all he would be able to get in that life; it asked him to spend the rest of his life in singing the Lord’s name and remembering him. He followed the instructions, and, after shedding his body, was born as the spiritual son of ब्रह्मा and got the status of the divine sage.
There is a close relationship between देवर्षि नारद and Sāmaveda as well as मुसिच्. It was he who authored the musical treatise known as Saṅgītamakaranda. He is the inventor of the vīṇā (lute) too. While moving among the three worlds, he assists those who are in distress. He preaches the knowledge of धर्म. Sometimes, he is supposed to correct and bring round people by encouraging them to quarrel! It is नारद who urged वाल्मीकि to compose Rāmāyaṇa and व्यास to write the Mahābhārata. Again, it is he who preached the भागवत-धर्म to प्रह्लाद while the latter was still in his मोथेर्’s womb. Śrī कृष्ण himself praises this great sage wholeheartedly (Mahābhārata—Śāntiparva 230).
It is very difficult to determine whether this नारद is a single individual or separate personalities. According to information available from various sources, his character may be described as follows: This great personage reached the most exalted station in life from the lowest, by self-effort as well as the grace of God and attained the position of देवर्षि. Veda-mantras found expression through his pure मिन्द्. A great ascetic, he led his life according to the principles that he preached. He moved among the three worlds in order to propagate the Lord’s name and preach devotion to God. Hundreds of people who came in touch with him changed their course to the path of religion and devotion.
The following are the works thought to be authored by नारद: Nārada भक्ति-sūtras, नारद स्मृति, Nāradīya शिक्षा, नारद Parivrājakopaniṣad, Nāradīya Purāṇa and Nārada Pāñcarātra.
WHAT IS A SŪTRA?
Nārada Bhaktisūtras is, like similar books of ancient times, in the form of sūtras. The following is the definition of a sūtra:
‘Those who know sūtras consider a sūtra as that (a brief sentence) which contains very few letters, gives rise to no doubt (has a clear meaning), includes the essence of all related topics and does not have any superfluous words.’
Sūtra also means a thread. As various flowers are strung together by a thread to make a garland, or, as a necklace in which several beads are strung together, information in this area of knowledge is collected from various sources and is arranged in the form of a compilation. A sūtra that consists of very few letters can be easily memorized. Perhaps because there was no script in those days, or, even if it were there its use was not widespread, works of this kind were composed. Gradually, when writing became more popular, the expert disciples belonging to the particular schools wrote explanations of various kinds like bhāṣya, vyākhyāna, ṭikā, ṭippaṇi and वृत्ति on these sūtras. Had these commentaries not been available today, many ancient books would have become a meaningless jargon to us.
INTRODUCTION TO नारद BHAKTISŪTRAS
Nārada Bhaktisūtras is a brief work consisting only of 84 sūtras. It is a collection of नारद’s preachings taken from various sources and presenting them in the form of sūtras. The author of this work is unknown. According to some scholars, this was composed in 12th century A. D. But this is not definite. There is no commentary on it in Sanskrit, perhaps because its language is simple, beautiful and direct; if there is any commentary, it is unknown.
This is simpler and easier than the शाण्डिल्य Bhaktisūtras. Śaṇḍilya’s is, like other philosophical treatises, a work which is written in a terse language and contains arguments, for and against. It does not contain much material that is necessary or useful to the practitioners of devotion. In नारद’s work, on the other hand, the main subject under discussion is the practice of devotion. Not merely this, the readers are warned (sūs. 74-75) that they should not indulge in disputations!
THE SUBJECT AS ENUNCIATED IN THE PHILOSOPHICAL WORKS
We may, in general, present the subjects dealt with in the philosophical schools, especially those of Vedānta, as follows: pramāṇa (means of knowledge) and prameya (that which is to be known). प्रत्यक्ष, अनुमान, āgama (direct experience, inference and scriptures)—these three are the प्रमाणस् that are generally acceptable.
The subjects mentioned under prameya are: ईश्वर, जीव, jagat (God, सोउल् and the world), the aim of life, spiritual practices, the nature of लिबेरतिओन् and the characteristics of a liberated man.
If this work of नारद is looked at from this viewpoint, we cannot consider it as a work of devotional philosophy. There is nothing of pramāṇa here. In the same way, nothing is mentioned about the च्रेअतिओन् of the world and the nature of jīvātman (limited self).
It is with some difficulty that things like nature and characteristics of God can be discovered in it. So too about the objective of life. But there is a great deal of information regarding devotional practices, the nature and features of devotion, and about the ideal devotee. Hence, it will not be wrong if it is called a treatise on devotional practices. If experienced scholars could blend the philosophical principles of the Śāṇḍilya Bhaktisūtras and the spiritual practices as found in the Nārada Bhaktisūtras and try to compose a work of devotional philosophy, it would be a great service rendered to भागवत-धर्म (or religion of devotion). Here is an attempt to present the information about this work in a systematic manner.
ĪŚVARA
The objective of human life is the realization of God. This God exists in everyone’s heart very close to us, the innermost self (sū. 2). He dislikes pride and egoism. Instead, he wants and likes humility in his devotees (sū. 27). He is also called ‘Bhagavān.’ When the devotees listen to his virtues, sing in praise of him and pray to him, he receives these offerings and appears before them and blesses them, because he is full of grace (sūs. 37, 38, 40, 80). When once he appears before us, everything will have been achieved. What नारद has preached has also originally come from him (sū. 84).
BHAKTI
The easiest (sū. 58) and the best instrument (sūs. 25, 26, 30, 59, 60) to have God-realization is devotion. This is superior to ज्ञान (knowledge), योग (meditation), कर्म (rituals) and such other spiritual practices. This, indeed, is the result of all these practices.
This भक्ति may be divided into two aspects—parābhakti and aparābhakti. Aparā-भक्ति can be further divided into gauṇī भक्ति and mukhya भक्ति. While parābhakti is the aim, aparābhakti is the means to obtain it.
Parābhakti
Parābhakti is the manifestation of the great bliss that results from God-realization. It is of the nature of great love for God. It is full of bliss like nectar; also, those who obtain this attain इम्मोर्तलित्य् and लिबेरतिओन् (sūs. 2, 3). Since this has been described as of the nature of great love, could it not be considered as a form of desire like worldly love? No, it is that which checks and destroys all desires (sū. 7). When parābhakti is aroused in the heart, it may find expression in many ways; for instance—particular attachment to rites of worship, avidity to listen to stories about the Lord, surrendering the fruit of all the work done, and great longing (sū. 16-19).
Aparābhakti
There are two stages in aparābhakti. The initial one is gauṇībhakti and the higher one is mukhyabhakti or premā-भक्ति.
Gauṇībhakti
Gauṇībhakti is of three kinds: sāttvika, rājasika and tāmasika; or आर्त-भक्ति, arthārthibhakti and jijñāsubhakti (sū. 56). Practice of this gauṇībhakti is easy. It is the natural love that resides in the heart and needs to be directed towards the Lord and hence, it needs no proof. By practice, gradually one can attain peace and great bliss (sūs. 58-60). This gauṇī-भक्ति appears in eleven different ways like, for example, to be greatly attached to the noble virtues and greatness of God, to be engaged in His worship and so on.
Mukhyabhakti
The practice of gauṇībhakti gradually leads us towards mukhyabhakti. This is otherwise called premābhakti or ekānta-भक्ति. This is the penultimate state of parābhakti, the last but one step. If one gets this, the manifestation of parābhakti will not be far away. This mukhyabhakti or premābhakti is experienced inside the heart. But it cannot be described in words. This is like a dumb person eating a tasty dish (sūs. 51-52). Though this is a rare experience, it finds expression in advanced practitioners (sū. 53). The words and actions, the feelings and thoughts of that lucky individual who has had this subtle experience, which is beyond the three guṇas, devoid of all worldly desires and which is continuously growing, are suffused with that love (sūs. 54, 55).
BHAKTISĀDHANA
Various kinds of instructions and guidance on devotional practices are found aplenty in this work. The practitioner of devotion should always give importance to the scriptures because they have originated from the ṛṣis, munis and great men. If he does not give them prominence, there is a possibility of his slipping off the track of practice (sūs. 12, 13).
But the scriptures that the practitioners of devotion should give the greatest importance to, are the devotional scriptures. He should study them and reflect on them in his मिन्द्. He should perform those duties preached in them which will help devotion to grow. There is no point in arguing with others in this regard (sūs. 74-76).
The devotee should renounce those duties—whether worldly or scriptural—which come in the way of his practice and perform the rest with the conviction that they are an offering to God (sūs. 8-11). As the body is a valuable instrument to be used in the path of practice, he should protect it well (sū. 14).
A great obstruction to spiritual life is the attraction towards sense objects. Hence the devotee has, willy-nilly, to attempt to renounce externally the pleasures born of sense objects and, in his own मिन्द्, his attachment to them. An easy solution to this problem is continuous prayer and remembrance as well as the company of great men and, thereby, their grace (sūs. 35-42). It is as much necessary to renounce the company of the wicked as cultivate the company of the great. In the company of the wicked, there is every possibility of bad सṁस्कारस् (mental proclivities) like desire and anger in the devotee’s मिन्द् rising up (sūs. 43-45). Wicked company does not necessarily mean company of wicked persons. The sense objects that help stimulate the मिन्द् and give rise to desire, greed, अथेइस्म्, enmity and anger are also wicked company. We should not even listen to such things (sū. 63).
Māyā or इल्लुसिओन् is the captivating power of God; to cross it is very difficult. But, unless it is crossed, there can be no लिबेरतिओन्. With this purpose, the devotee should, apart from shunning the company of the wicked and cultivating that of the noble, practise a few more things. Praying to the Lord in solitude, surrendering his thoughts about his security to God Himself, giving up actions born of desires and offering the fruit of the rest of the things he does to God, to free himself from the bondage of the world and so on—these are the other practices (sūs. 46-50). When he obtains through these, an unceasing devotion, he will not only cross māyā with the grace of God, but achieve the power to help others to cross it too.
The devotee surrenders himself totally to the Lord. Hence he should not bother about this world or the next. This does not mean that he should give up worldly and scripturally prescribed actions. While engaging himself in these actions, if he offers their fruit to the Supreme Self, devotion gradually gets ripened (sūs. 61-62).
Desire, anger and such other passions are great obstacles on the path of spiritual practice. It is, indeed, very arduous to fight them directly and win. Hence, नारद suggests a solution that is easy and shrewd, to direct them towards the Lord Himself! The gopis turned their cravings towards कृष्ण and killed them; in the same way, we too could destroy them (sū. 64).
The devotee who is engaged in this internal battle should incessantly be praying to the Lord without wasting even a moment of his time. As an aid and complement to this, he should practise non-violence, truth, mercy and such other noble virtues (sūs. 77-79). If he continues to pray to the Supreme Self in this way, the latter will appear before the devotee very quickly and grant him His experience, bliss and लिबेरतिओन्.
THE CHARACTERISTICS OF A LIBERATED DEVOTEE
The man who attains लिबेरतिओन् (i.e., parābhakti) is a siddha-पुरुष. As he is ever-contented, he doesn’t crave for anything. As he is totally blissful, there is no trace of sorrow in him. As he sees his beloved Supreme Self everywhere, he does not hate anyone. As, again, he is contented always, he does not need to engage himself in any action to satisfy his desires. Sometimes, he becomes rapt in parābhakti and like a bee that has sucked honey a little too much, he stands lost in himself. When he is conscious, he experiences that sublime love and sees the Lord everywhere. He listens only to things about Him, he talks and thinks about Him alone. When he meets other devotees, all of them converse about God alone, shedding blissful tears and thus spend their time (sū. 68). As he has surrendered to God everything that belongs to him even after he has experienced parābhakti, this devotee will continue to engage himself in worldly and religious activities in order to guide others. Scriptures and actions become holier because of this (sūs. 4-6; 55, 61, 62, 68).
These devotees do not recognize any differences among themselves as they belong to the ‘caste’ of the devotees; that is, the ‘caste’ of God. They do not recognize differences even with others (sū. 72). Such great devotees sanctify their families. They make holy pilgrim centres holier when they visit them; not merely that, they make the whole earth more sacred. Looking at them, manes and gods dance with glee (sūs. 69-71).
CONCLUSION
Nārada has not preached this devotional scripture merely with his intellectual power. He obtained it directly from शिव-महादेव Himself. There are very great men like Sanatkumāra, व्यास, शुक, शाण्डिल्य, बलि, हनुमान् and विभीषण who belong to this great भक्ति-tradition. Forever they live in God. Hence, with one मिन्द् they have spread broadcast their preachings, unmindful of the frivolous criticism levelled against them by uncultured people. Those who have complete faith and trust in this devotional work and practise what is preached in it, will definitely attain the Supreme Self dearest to their hearts.

narabali
(‘human sacrifice’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘Puruṣamedha’ (‘sacrificing a human being’) occurs in Āpastamba Śrautasūtras (20.24, 25) and Baudhāyana Śrautasūtras (24.11). It is a type of सोमयाग spread over five days.
Whether a पुरुष (human being) was actually sacrificed or whether the whole act had been symbolical, is difficult to ascertain.
There are references to नरबलि in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.2.3,6) and the Taittirīya Saṁhitā (2.2.2,4) also.
According to one view, since a large quantity of human and animal bones were recovered at the site of excavations at Kauśāmbi (the modern Kosam, about 50 kms. [31 miles] to the east of Allahabad in Uttar Pradesh) including an ancient altar, this sacrifice must have existed.
According to other scholars, the rite was only symbolical. After the पर्यग्निकरण rite—wherein the आग्नीध्र priest goes round the human beings and the animals with a lighted torch—the human beings are released and only goats are sacrificed (vide P. V. Kane, History of Dharmaśāstra Vol. 3, Poona, Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, 1946; pages 961-2).
In the पुराणस् we do come across the practice of नरबलि by certain aboriginal cults (vide Bhāgavata 5.9.15 to 17). The great spiritual teacher शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820) is said to have been approached for sacrifice by the Kāpālikas. He was later on saved by his disciple पद्मपाद.
We find a reference to पुरुषमेध in the story of हरिश्चन्द्र as given in the Bhāgavata (9.7) wherein शुनश्शेफ was about to be offered to वरुण but was saved by his prayer to that deity.
The rite might have existed at least in the most aboriginal tribes.
